newsitem.title: USA: Bail set for alleged Cosby extortionists.
newsitem.headline: Bail set for alleged Cosby extortionists.

text.p: A federal magistrate judge approved bail Friday for a man and a woman accused of trying to extort $40 million from entertainer Bill Cosby but they are not expected to be released until at least Monday.

Autumn Jackson, 22, and Jose Medina, 51, were arrested last weekend on charges they demanded money from Cosby to refrain from selling a tabloid newspaper a story alleging that Jackson is the entertainer's illegitimate daughter.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Andrew Peck approved a bail package for each defendant that includes a $250,000 bond co-signed by two financially responsible people. The defendants cannot be released until federal prosecutors are satisfied the co-signers can secure the bonds and the process is expected to delay their release until at least early next week.
According to court papers, Jackson was one of many young people for whom Cosby paid educational expenses for several years. He has denied Jackson is his daughter.
Federal prosecutors have said there was no evidence the scheme was connected with the murder of Cosby's son Ennis, killed by a gunman in Los Angeles Jan 16.

If Jackson can meet the bail terms, she will be released to the custody of her grandmother in California. Neither prosecutors nor her defence lawyer would provide the grandmother's name or location. Peck also ordered that Jackson undergo drug testing and treatment if necessary.

Both defendants were prohibited from contacting Cosby, his family, his representatives or CBS. CBS Evening News reported Tuesday that the CBS television network, which airs the situation comedy "Cosby," had also been a target of the extortion attempt.

The terms for Medina are somewhat more stringent because prosecutors revealed during the bail hearing that he was on probation for an unrelated crime when the alleged extortion attempt occurred. He must wear an electronic monitoring device and his bond must be secured by $50,000 in cash or property.
If he can meet the terms, he will be released to the custody of his employer Dixie Dunn, an occupational therapist in whose home he has been living since at least 1989.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Lewis Liman said Medina had been convicted of fraud in Kansas for misrepresenting that he could obtain a loan for an individual. He said Medina obtained a $50,000 advance fee and pocketed the money. He would not provide further details.

Neil Checkman, Medina's lawyer, told Peck his client had suffered a severe head injury in 1983 that resulted in memory loss. Medina, who describes himself as an Orthodox Jew, cannot remember where he was born or where his family live, his lawyer said.
Checkman said Medina met Dunn when she provided therapy for his head injury. He now works as an equipment technician by adapting utensils for Dunn's disabled patients.

The lawyer said Dunn had sent Medina to California to help her research a children's television project. He said Medina met Jackson while he was staying at the Burbank Holiday Inn, where she was a clerk.
